strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real VAD deployment bottlenecks (scarcity of real abnormal data)
Thoughtfully designed multi-component pipeline combining CLIP selection, VLM refinement, and domain-aligned adaptation
Strong result on ShanghaiTech showing synthetic anomalies can exceed real anomalies in performance (98.2% vs 97.6% best Real/Real baseline)
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating contributions of each component and showing sensitivity to number of synthetic clips
Solid experimental methodology with proper separation of Real/Pseudo comparisons and evaluation on two established benchmarks
Good qualitative analysis with diverse pseudo-anomaly examples and feature analysis validating magnitude alignment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—individual components (CLIP selection, VLM refinement, domain adversarial training) apply existing techniques; contribution is primarily engineering their combination
Performance gains are inconsistent and marginal: +0.6% on ShanghaiTech (within potential noise) and −4.1% gap on UCF-Crime vs. best baselines; no statistical significance testing provided
Generalization concerns: evaluation limited to only two surveillance datasets with no cross-dataset testing or exploration of other anomaly detection domains
Insufficient analysis of pseudo-anomaly quality: no perceptual studies, limited discussion of anomaly type-specific challenges, and no systematic failure mode analysis to explain 4.1% UCF-Crime gap

Design choices lack principled justification: DARM formulation appears empirically driven, no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (λ_da, gradient reversal), and domain alignment motivation could be more rigorous
Computational cost and practical trade-offs underexplored in main paper: generation requires ~30 hours per 30 clips, but cost-benefit vs. real data collection not clearly quantified
Prompt engineering aspects underspecified: limited sensitivity analysis for initial prompts, single LLM choice (Qwen), and potential variability in refined prompts not explored
Comparison fairness: Real Normal + Pseudo Abnormal training differs from Real Normal + Real Abnormal baselines; missing comparisons with recent WVAD methods and other synthetic data approaches

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem with genuine deployment constraints (privacy, scarcity, cost of abnormal footage collection)
Novel empirical discovery of spatiotemporal magnitude bias in synthesized anomalies, well-documented with quantitative evidence (~20× norm inflation on ShanghaiTech)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, generation quality metrics, open-set generalization, and qualitative comparisons; particularly strong open-set results (72.50→89.08 on XD-Violence)
Sensible CA-PAG design using CLIP-guided image selection with positive/negative balancing and VLM-based prompt refinement, avoiding manual prompt search
Strong empirical results: surpasses WVAD baselines on ShanghaiTech (+0.6%) and XD-Violence (+0.9%), exceeds UVAD SOTA on UCF-Crime (+1.9%)
Well-organized presentation with clear figures, comprehensive supplementary material including hyperparameters and prompts, supporting reproducibility
Pragmatic contribution: trades hard-to-collect real abnormal data for readily available pretrained knowledge—a reasonable tradeoff for real-world deployment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (CLIP retrieval, VLM refinement, video diffusion, DANN-based domain alignment from Ganin et al. 2016, usage-aware updates from UR-DMU [36]) rather than developing fundamentally new methods

Unfair comparison with UVAD baselines: paper acknowledges supervision level inequality but insufficiently addresses that PA-VAD leverages massive pretrained knowledge (Wan 2.2, Qwen3, CLIP, Qwen2.5-VL) while UVAD methods have no such access; frames this as trading one constraint for another but comparison merits more nuanced discussion

Significant performance limitation on UCF-Crime: 82.5% vs 87.0% UR-DMU (Real/Real), a 4.5 point gap attributed to difficulty synthesizing extended temporal anomalies; raises concerns about generalization to longer-form behaviors

Shallow magnitude bias analysis: paper documents the phenomenon (Table 1) but root-cause investigation is superficial ('synthesis artifacts' explanation); missing investigation into why large norms correlate with specific artifact types, or whether norm inflation could be decoupled from quality issues

No human evaluation of pseudo-anomaly quality: generation metrics (FVD, KVD) don't capture semantic fidelity; lacks domain expert assessment of whether synthesized behaviors are behaviorally realistic or semantically coherent
Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: numerous parameters (λ₁, λ₂, λ_da, λ_dist, β) with dataset-dependent values; minimal ablation on hyperparameter choices or selection methodology

High generation computational cost (~30-55 hours on dual RTX 6000 Ada) may limit reproducibility and accessibility for resource-constrained settings; not thoroughly discussed relative to annotation time for real data
Limited failure mode analysis: shoplifting example (Fig. 2f) shows poor quality but no per-class performance breakdown identifying which anomaly types are systematically harder to synthesize
Missing per-class performance analysis and statistical significance testing: no confidence intervals, error bars, or per-dataset-per-class breakdown
Marginal advantage over SF-VAD/FPL: PA-VAD (98.2%) vs SF-VAD (98.4%) on ShanghaiTech despite SF-VAD using real abnormal videos, undermining the practical value proposition
